body:
## The check that catches agent failures can also train them

In our second post on ThinkingBox, we look at expanded model evaluations, the price of dependable runs, and reinforcement learning on terminal-state rewards.

A traveler asks a support agent to switch a $1,450 hotel booking from a suite to a deluxe room. Company policy states that the change requires a manager’s approval first. In 15 of 20 attempts, the open-weight model Qwen3.8-27B made the change anyway. It updated the room, refunded money, marked the support ticket solved, and told the traveler it was done.

While that may sound like good customer service, it’s a violation of company policy.

In our first post , the failure ran the other way. An agent told a traveler their quiet-room request had been added, while the booking’s special requests field stayed empty. We built ThinkingBox to catch both kinds of failure. It runs an agent in an isolated, stateful environment, lets a simulated user answer its questions, and then checks the records the agent left behind rather than simply trusting what it said.

Since then, we’ve expanded the evaluation to 18 models and published our method and results in a paper . This post covers three things we learned:

• Average success and repeatable success rank models differently

• The cheapest successful attempt is not the cheapest dependable task

• The same check that grades an agent can be used to train it

After 50 steps of reinforcement learning on tasks outside the benchmark, the same 27B model left that booking and its payments untouched in all 20 attempts. Across the 507-task benchmark, the number of tasks it passed on every one of 20 attempts rose from 38 to 107.

## Most failed runs looked finished

The first question we asked of the larger run was how often a failure would be visible without checking the final state of the database where the operation is recorded (the environment in RL terminology).

Our paper compares the executable verdict against three weaker signals on a common set of tasks across 12 models. Of 121,680 valid trials, 79,853 failed the executable check. In 67.24% of those failures, the agent still ended with a final response that signaled completion without asking a question, called at least one tool that changes state, and received no explicit error in its final tool response.

By those signals, which a transcript or tool-call log can show, about two in three failed runs looked complete.

But the records told a different story. In 98.95% of failures, the final database differed from the expected one. In 77.61%, a field held the wrong value. In 43.30%, the agent made a change nobody asked for, and in 25.36%, a required change never happened.

The paper also labels each failed run with one dominant failure signature. Averaged across the evaluated models, 79.9% of failures were tool-usage failures: the agent hit a tool error, a failed precondition, or an empty lookup and didn’t recover, sometimes carrying on as if the action had been taken successfully. These labels describe what the trace shows, not a proven root cause. But they point to fixes that don’t need a new model: classify tool and system errors so retries target the recoverable ones, keep the tool surface to what the workflow needs, and require human approval for changes that are expensive to reverse. We haven’t measured how much each of these helps. Training, which the rest of this post covers, is one way to improve repeatability, not the only one.

That result shaped everything else discussed in this post. We use the task’s executable verdict throughout, primarily based on whether the records match, with narrow response-rubric checks where required.

## Average success and repeated success rank models differently

Running every task 20 times gives three different views of the same model:

• Pass@1: The share of all 10,140 attempts (507 tasks x 20) that passed. This is the same as mean pass rate.

• At least once: Tasks the model passed in at least one of its k=20 attempts.

• Pass^20: The share of tasks the model passed in all 20 recorded attempts. Tables also show the corresponding task counts.

Since our first post, we expanded the comparison and trained a checkpoint of our own, described later in this post. Table 1 updates the leaderboard with selected models from that evaluation: pass@1 by domain and overall and pass^20 with its task count.

Kimi-K3 passed 476 of 507 tasks at least once, more than any other model shown in Figure 2. It passed only 68 tasks on all 20 attempts. Claude Opus 5 passed fewer tasks at least once (401) but passed 241 on all 20. One model finds more solutions. The other repeats its solutions more reliably. In other words, one model is better at exploring the search space and looking for innovative solutions at the expense of higher variability while the other is better at exploiting known solution strategies.

Average accuracy doesn’t settle the question either. GPT-6 Astra scored 58.31% on pass@1, about seven points below GPT-5.4 at 65.36%. It still passed 231 tasks on all 20 attempts, compared with 128 for GPT-5.4. We also ran Claude Opus 5.5, which doesn’t appear in the paper, with the same protocol. It scored 0.66 points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1 and passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all 20 attempts.

Which column matters depends on the job. If a person reviews every result, a model that eventually finds an answer may be enough. If an agent changes production records without review, the pass^20 column is closer to what you need. It’s still an observation over 20 attempts—not a guarantee about attempt 21—although increasing the number of attempts provides an increasingly better estimate.
